alt: Five layers of human rights rules, each with an example: the Convention text (Article 10.1 and 10.2), Strasbourg case law (Handyside v UK), the Human Rights Act 1998 (the section 6 duty), statute (PACE 1984) and common law (Entick v Carrington; Derbyshire CC v Times Newspapers). Below: Derbyshire stops a council suing for defamation, and Simms sets out the principle of legality.
caption: Convention, case law, the HRA, statute and common law each supply part of the rules.

after: ## The five rights at a glance
alt: Three columns. Absolute rights, such as Article 3, allow no balancing. Limited rights, Article 2 (life) and Article 5 (liberty and security), can be restricted only in the ways the Article lists. Qualified rights, Articles 8, 10 and 11, can be restricted if prescribed by law, for a legitimate aim, and necessary in a democratic society.
caption: Limited rights use the Article’s own list; qualified rights use the three-part test.

after: ## Principles that apply to every right
alt: Two panels. Negative obligation: the state must not interfere with an individual’s right without justification. Positive obligation: the state must step in to protect an individual, including against a private person. Examples: X and Y v Netherlands (Article 8), Osman v UK (Article 2) and protecting a lawful demonstration from counter-protesters (Article 11).
caption: Every right restrains the state; many also require it to protect people from others.

after: ## Principles that apply to every right
alt: Five interpretation principles: living instrument (Tyrer v UK, birching), practical and effective rights (Airey v Ireland, access to court), autonomous meaning (Engel v Netherlands, “criminal charge”), the margin of appreciation, and proportionality.
caption: The Convention is read as a living, practical document with its own meanings.

after: ## Principles that apply to every right
alt: Left: vertical effect, where an individual relies on Convention rights against the state or a public authority under HRA section 6. Right: indirect horizontal effect, where a court, itself a public authority, develops the law between private parties such as a model and a newspaper (Campbell v MGN). Article 14 on discrimination must be argued with another Article (A v Home Secretary, with Article 5).
caption: Rights bind the state directly and reach private disputes through the courts.

after: ## A method for any human rights problem
alt: Six numbered steps: identify the right and Article; classify it as limited or qualified; ask whether it is engaged; identify the interference or failure to protect; test justification by the listed exceptions or the three-part test; then enforcement and remedy.
caption: Identify, classify, engaged, interference, justified, remedy.

alt: Sam’s facts mapped to rights. Intercepting his calls engages Article 8, where a vague by-law may fail “in accordance with the law”. Banning the march and arresting him engage Articles 10 and 11, where a total ban is hard to justify. Holding him 40 hours engages Article 5, needing a 5.1(c) ground and prompt appearance under 5.3. Remedy under HRA sections 6 to 8.
caption: Each fact engages its own Article, and each Article has its own test.
